newsitem.title: ECUADOR: FEATURE - Ecuador's rocking president does it his way.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ecuador's rocking president does it his way.

text.p: The president shaved off his Charlie Chaplin moustache live on television. Then he released a rock 'n' roll CD and had lunch at his palace with Lorena Bobbit, famed for slashing off her husband's penis.

Ecuador's President Abdala Bucaram, a genial, portly man who disdains suits for shirtsleeves and calls himself the "superhero" of the poor, is not your average world leader. "I do whatever the hell I like," he declared while campaigning.

Despite being accused of being, among other things, a drunkard and a drug trafficker by his opponents, Bucaram's populist campaign culminated in a July 7 victory based on massive support from the poor and Ecuador's native Indians.
The quiet Andean nation has not been the same since. Postponing major economic announcements until later in the year, Bucaram has gleefully pumped up the populist volume.

The presidential compact disc, entitled "A Madman in Love," was not long in coming. His ample abdomen clad in a flashy black shirt and flanked by young female backup singers in tight-fitting midriff outfits, he belted out his 13 original tunes live in concert in the port city of Guayaquil.
Untroubled by any desire for a statesmanlike image, the 44-year-old Bucaram boasted he had always used rock 'n' roll to seduce women, including his wife, with whom he has four children.

Bobbit got a free Bucaram CD when she came to lunch at the palace. She earned the honour by becoming one of the world's most famous Ecuadorans in 1993, when she mutilated her husband John Wayne Bobbit in revenge for his allegedly raping and abusing her. She was found not guilty and he, after a surgical reattachment, has gone on to a career in X-rated films.

Bucaram hailed her before the press as a defender of women's rights. "You are a person who knows how to defend her principles and values," he said, adding "You look a lot prettier in person than you do on television."

The president basked in feminist sentiment just days after one of his top officials, Energy Minister Alfredo Adum, told a magazine he would like to live without clothes and prey on women like a caveman.

But the unusual behaviour of Bucaram and his team does not seem to have done any him political harm. A private poll showed that 53 percent of Ecuadorans think he did a good job in his first 60 days of office. And, clowning aside, Bucaram is considered an astute politician in a long-established Latin American populist mould.

He declared soon after taking office that he would hold regular lunches at the palace for leaders of the country's indigenous groups and that he would set up a $250 million social programme focused on housing, education and nutrition. At the same time, he sent a reassuring message to foreign investors, naming former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, renowned for fighting inflation, as an adviser.
"Bucaram is a phenomenum. As long as there is poverty, there'll be populism," political analyst Luis Eladio Proano said.

"What he does is to systematically break the rules of the game," said sociologist Rafael Guerrero. "One characteristic of Bucaram's populist style is that it polarises society, it polarises it into rich and poor, common people and the oligarchy."

Trained as a lawyer, with a postgraduate degree in physical education, Bucaram began his political career in the Guayaquil town hall, where his duties included maintaining the port city's morals. Naturally, he went about it in his own distinctive way. Locals tell how Bucaram zipped around town on a motorcycle, intercepting young women and personally unstitching the hems of their miniskirts to make them longer.
As a politician he swiftly mastered the common touch but he twice failed as a presidential candidate despite election stunts such as jumping out of a helicopter dressed as Batman.

The superhero of the poor is facing a rough ride. There have been spats with the interior minister over government policy and oil workers have started legal action against the energy minister, alleging corruption.
"I deserve to be called a madman, as I am a passionate man who loves his people blindly," Bucaram once said. "But I am a man with a lot of common sense."
